findings.title: Index creation without CONCURRENTLY locks writes on a large table
findings.explanation: A plain CREATE INDEX on PostgreSQL takes a SHARE lock on `events`, blocking all INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE for the whole build. An events/activity table is typically large and write-heavy, so this can cause an outage or request pile-up during deploy. Use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS events_project_id_idx ON events (project_id, id DESC);`. Note that CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block, so make sure the migration tool is configured to run this file outside a transaction (e.g. a no-transaction directive in your tool), and be aware that a failed concurrent build leaves an INVALID index that must be dropped and recreated.

findings.title: Not idempotent / no IF NOT EXISTS
findings.explanation: If the migration is retried after a partial failure, or the index was already created manually in production to relieve the problem, the migration will fail with 'relation already exists'. Add IF NOT EXISTS, and consider including a documented rollback (DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS events_project_id_idx) if your migration tooling supports down migrations.

findings.title: Index may be redundant or not match the actual query
findings.explanation: The PR does not show the query, so it is unverified that the index matches it. If an existing index on `(project_id)` exists, it becomes redundant (the new composite covers it) and should be dropped to reduce write overhead and storage. Also, the 'sequential scan per project' claim should be backed by EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) before/after output. If the query filters on additional columns (e.g. event type, tenant/org, or a created_at range) or orders by something other than id, the index may not be used as expected. Postgres can scan a (project_id, id) index backward, so `id DESC` is not strictly needed unless mixed ordering is used; it is harmless but worth confirming.

findings.title: Write overhead and index size not discussed
findings.explanation: Every insert into `events` will now maintain an additional index. For a high-volume append-only table this is usually acceptable, but the PR description should mention the expected index size and insert-rate impact. Consider also whether the endpoint uses keyset pagination on `id` (`WHERE project_id = $1 AND id < $cursor ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT n`); if it uses OFFSET, the index helps less for deep pages.

```diff
@@ -0,0 +1 @@
+CREATE INDEX events_project_id_idx ON events (project_id, id DESC);
```
